world.bio: I'm Tessa, thirty-three, a social work graduate in Western Sydney. Two years ago I started a sewing circle with women from Afghanistan and South Sudan who had been resettled in the area. I speak a little Dari, mostly hand gestures, and I've learned more about sleeves than I ever planned to. By day I work part-time at a community legal centre; by night and on weekends I'm planning a wedding on a shoestring and training as a volunteer firefighter. My housemate is moving out next month.
skills_assets: Coordinates a sewing circle for refugee women in Western Sydney, about nine regular members
Four domestic sewing machines (two donated, two bought second-hand), one overlocker on loan
Contacts at a settlement services agency, a local council community development officer, and two churches
A small grant covering fabric, thread and needles for twelve months
Social work degree and four years of casework experience with newly arrived families
A shared WhatsApp group in which half the messages are voice notes and half are photos of finished garments
Basic Dari phrases and a laminated picture dictionary for pattern-making terms

projects.name: Western Sydney sewing circle
projects.text: Every Thursday and Saturday morning, nine of us meet in Farida's lounge room in Blacktown. Four machines, a cutting table made from a door on trestles, an ironing board that tips if you lean on it. The women are from Afghanistan and South Sudan; some were seamstresses at home, some have never touched a machine. Two new members joined last month and now there is literally no room: we take turns, and someone is always standing. The women have started asking about taking small alteration orders from neighbours, hems and zips and school uniforms, so they can earn a little. I don't know how to make that work yet.

projects.name: Space and grant search
projects.text: The grant is small and covers fabric and thread only. There is no venue budget and no hall of our own. We would need a weekday-morning space with power points for six machines, mostly because the women have kids in school and mornings are the only time they are free. I have emailed three councils and a church; so far, kind replies, no keys.

projects.name: Wedding on a shoestring
projects.text: Marco and I are marrying in March at his aunt's backyard in Penrith. Budget is $6,000 and I am making my own dress, which the women in the circle are strongly opinionated about.

notes.text: Thursday circle. Farida made tea in a pot big enough for twelve and we drank it standing up. Nyabol is learning to thread the machine herself and when the bobbin finally caught she shouted something in Dinka that made everyone laugh. I have no idea what it meant but the room felt like a room. Then I counted: eleven women, four machines, one door-table. We are bursting.

Rostered for fire brigade training. Ran in full gear for 20 minutes and nearly threw up. Captain says I have good instincts. I told him I just have a good fear of being useless. He laughed, but I wasn't joking.

Housemate Jess told me she's moving out at the end of October. I said that's fine, genuinely, and then I lay in bed doing sums about rent. Marco says move in with him early. I said no, I need my own mess for one more year.

Spoke to the council officer about a hall. She said the community centre on Main Street has a room free on Tuesday mornings but it's $38 an hour. We have no hourly budget. She suggested a grant application that opens in February. February is a long way off.

Sat with Hasina and tried to explain 'alteration' through a video of someone taking up trousers. She understood in ten seconds and then said, in Dari, something that Farida translated as 'we can do this better than the shop'. They can. I've seen the hems.

Wedding dress fitting #2 in the lounge room. Six women pinned me like a hedgehog. Nyabol says the neckline should be higher. Farida says lower. I stood there for forty minutes in a half-made dress feeling loved and slightly hostage.

Mum called. She asked why I'm spending my weekends on 'a hobby that doesn't pay'. I said it isn't a hobby, it's the only thing that makes me feel like my degree wasn't wasted. She said that's a lot to put on sewing. Maybe it is.

The overlocker on loan has to go back in three weeks. We will lose it. Without it, the alterations idea is dead on arrival, since raw edges fray. Need to find another or buy one. A decent one is $480 second-hand. Our petty cash is $63.

Spring. Farida's lounge room smelled of cardamom and hot iron. The window was open. The women were singing something slow while pressing seams, and for a second I thought: if there were a hall with real light, this is what it would look like every week.

messages.text:
Farida: Tessa, new lady is coming Saturday, is that ok?
Me: Of course. Bring her. We will find a chair.
Farida: We have no chair. She can sit on my sofa.
Me: Then the sofa it is.

Dana: Tuesday mornings only, $38 an hour. Sorry, Tessa.
Me: Thank you for checking. Any chance of a community rate?
Dana: I'll ask. No promises.
Me: That's more than anyone else has offered.

Marco: Mum wants to know if the women would like to cater the engagement lunch.
Me: They would love it, but they'd want to be paid properly.
Marco: Obviously. Ask them.
Me: I will.

Jess: Sorry again about moving out. I found a place in Newtown.
Me: Don't apologise. I'll find someone.
Jess: Not a flatmate who sews, I hope.
Me: Hard to say. I'm recruiting.

Mum: Dad says come Sunday, he's doing a roast.
Me: I'll bring the dress to show you.
Mum: Don't tell me it's pinned by strangers.
Me: Not strangers. Women who love me.

relations.about: Hosts the circle in her lounge room; former dressmaker in Kabul.
South Sudanese member, learning to thread the machine herself.
Afghan member who understands alterations instantly.

constraints: Women can only meet weekday mornings because of school drop-offs
No venue budget; the grant covers fabric and thread only
The women should be paid fairly if they do alterations; no charity framing
Tessa works part-time and has volunteer firefighter commitments on weekends
sensitive: Feels her degree would be wasted without the circle
Anxious about money after Jess moves out
Worries the loaned overlocker will go back and the circle will lose momentum
